Disputes arising under the license are subject to mediation under the rules of the World Intellectual Property Organization. These updates supplement the 2016 consolidated guidelines. The recommendations are based on systematic reviews of evidence, including considerations of values, preferences, feasibility, acceptability, and cost. The guidelines emphasize a public health approach and a woman-centered model of care, respecting women's autonomy and providing them with information and options to make informed decisions. Key updates include the recommendation of dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimens as the preferred first-line treatment for people living with HIV, including adults, adolescents, and children with approved DTG dosing. However, caution is advised for women and adolescent girls of childbearing potential due to a potential association between DTG use during the periconception period and an increased risk of neural tube defects in infants. DTG is considered safe when initiated later in pregnancy, after the first trimester. Women who do not wish to become pregnant can use DTG with reliable contraception, as there are no known drug interactions between DTG and hormonal contraceptives. For second-line treatment, DTG combined with an optimized nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) backbone is recommended for individuals whose non-DTG-based regimens are failing. Alternative third-drug options include atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r), darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r), lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r), and raltegravir (RAL). The guidelines also introduce the use of an indeterminate range for nucleic acid-based early infant diagnosis assays to improve diagnostic accuracy. This range accounts for viral copy levels that are too low to be definitively diagnosed as positive. The target audience for these guidelines includes national HIV program managers, clinicians, health workers, laboratory service managers, and organizations providing financial and technical support to HIV programs in lowand middle-income countries.
